article.title: Node.js, ASP.NET Core 2.3, CPython's JIT and Kubernetes' kube-dns Each Carry a Different Notice: Calendar, Policy Minimum, Council Window, Versions
article.summary: Sources on four 2026 changes show four notice models: a published Node.js calendar, Microsoft's 12-month minimum for ASP.NET Core 2.3, a Python Steering Council window for the JIT, and Kubernetes version targets.
article.body_markdown:
## Background

In 2026, four developer platforms and projects told their users that something was ending or narrowing. [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/en/blog/announcements/evolving-the-nodejs-release-schedule) said it would move from two major releases a year to one. [Microsoft](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet-core-2-3-end-of-support/) set an end-of-support date for ASP.NET Core 2.3. The [Python Steering Council](https://discuss.python.org/t/an-announcement-from-the-steering-council-regarding-the-jit-project/107638) set a six-month window after which CPython's experimental JIT compiler must leave the main branch unless a Python Enhancement Proposal (PEP) was accepted. The [Kubernetes project](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/26/kubernetes-v1-37-release/) gave version targets for retiring kube-dns packages and kube-proxy's IPVS mode. This Analysis compares how each change was announced, using the projects' own statements and reporting by [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/06/nodejs-release-changes/), [LWN.net](https://lwn.net/Articles/1102102/) and [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/software/2026/04/08/microsoft-calls-time-on-aspnet-core-23-on-net-framework/5223824). Reported facts come first; the comparison is kept in a separate section.

Each case started from a different rule. Microsoft's post says the [required notice](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet-core-2-3-end-of-support/) is 12 months, "as defined by the Microsoft Support Lifecycle Policy for products classified as “Tools.”" The Node.js post says its [previous schedule](https://nodejs.org/en/blog/announcements/evolving-the-nodejs-release-schedule) was 10 years old and was created during the io.js merger. The Steering Council wrote that when the JIT was merged into main [it entered as an experiment](https://discuss.python.org/t/an-announcement-from-the-steering-council-regarding-the-jit-project/107638), with PEP 744, which is Informational, as the only enhancement proposal written about it. The Kubernetes 1.37 post refers readers to the project's [deprecation and removal policy](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/26/kubernetes-v1-37-release/) for its process.

The Herald has covered parts of this before. A [News report](/article/2026-07/11-cpython-community-answers-steering-councils-six-month-jit-ultimatum-with-pep-836-a-path-to-a-supported-compiler) covered PEP 836's filing after the Council's six-month condition, and a [second](/article/2026-10/27-pep-836-authors-withdraw-their-cpython-jit-proposal-and-brett-cannon-says-the-withdrawal-means-the-jit-will-come-out-of-main) covered its withdrawal. An [earlier Analysis](/article/2026-11/03-kubernetes-137-sets-timelines-to-retire-ipvs-mode-and-kube-dns-packages-as-eks-and-gke-offer-rollback-and-eks-prices-extended-support) examined the Kubernetes 1.37 retirement timelines together with control-plane rollback and EKS extended-support pricing. This article does not repeat that analysis; it uses the Kubernetes timelines as one of four notice models.

## Current situation

**Node.js: a published calendar.** The project's post, which the page lists as [last updated March 10, 2026](https://nodejs.org/en/blog/announcements/evolving-the-nodejs-release-schedule), says that starting with 27.x Node.js will move from two major releases per year to one. As of October 2026, it lists one major release per year in April with promotion to LTS in October, every release becoming LTS, and an Alpha channel for early testing. For Node.js 27 it gives Alpha beginning in October 2026, 27.0.0 in April 2027, LTS in October 2027 and end of life in April 2030, and it calls Node.js 26 the last release line under the current model. The post also says the schedule "is not final and may be amended."

The post gives adoption as one reason ("Odd-numbered releases see minimal adoption. Most users wait for Long-Term Support.") and maintainer capacity as another ("Managing security releases across four or five active release lines has become difficult to sustain."). It says the change leaves Long-Term Support duration ["similar (30 months)"](https://nodejs.org/en/blog/announcements/evolving-the-nodejs-release-schedule). [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/06/nodejs-release-changes/), reporting on June 3, 2026, says the decision stemmed from a proposal opened by Node.js TSC member Rafael Gonzaga in July 2025, and that the GitHub discussion showed a tension between enterprise users who prefer long support windows and teams that upgrade frequently. InfoQ quotes Kevin Lentin, who described the view from inside a large corporation: "If we only get new LTS every 2 years, I'll go nuts waiting for features."

**ASP.NET Core 2.3: a policy minimum, and a date that moved.** Microsoft's post, by Daniel Roth, Principal Product Manager, and headed April 7, 2026, says [ASP.NET Core 2.3](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet-core-2-3-end-of-support/) will reach end of support on April 13, 2027, after which there will be no security patches, bug fixes or technical support. An update note on the post says the date was changed from April 7, 2027 to April 13, 2027 "to align with the Microsoft servicing release cycles." The post recommends upgrading to ".NET 10 (LTS)" and using GitHub Copilot modernization for the migration. Its stated reason is that continuing support "no longer aligns with our goal of helping customers move to a secure, modern, and actively maintained platform."

[The Register](https://www.theregister.com/software/2026/04/08/microsoft-calls-time-on-aspnet-core-23-on-net-framework/5223824), on April 8, 2026, reported the original date, April 7, 2027. It says version 2.3 was released in early 2025, that it is to be supported for fewer than two years, and that Microsoft justifies this by defining the framework as a "tool," a category whose only lifecycle requirement is a minimum of 12 months' notification; The Register writes that this "appears to be why the date set is one year from Roth's post yesterday." It reports that Roth gave the reason as the ongoing cost of maintenance and compliance, which "pulls resources from investment in our modern .NET platform." That wording does not appear in the [version of Microsoft's post](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet-core-2-3-end-of-support/) the Herald reviewed. The Register also quotes one user: "They showed a long-term commitment with 2.3 and now they're suddenly dropping it."

**CPython's JIT: a window described as an anchor.** The Steering Council's announcement, dated June 5, 2026, asked that [no new development on the JIT land on main](https://discuss.python.org/t/an-announcement-from-the-steering-council-regarding-the-jit-project/107638) until a PEP was accepted, while bug fixes and security fixes could continue. It called maintenance "a real concern for a subsystem of this size and complexity" and asked the PEP to set out a clear plan for sustaining the JIT. It set "a window of six months for a PEP to be submitted and resolved," after which, if no PEP was accepted, "the JIT code must be removed from the main branch and development must be continued outside the main Python repository." In the same thread, Pablo Galindo Salgado wrote that the Steering Council would be flexible and that the window was ["a first goal to anchor, not a bureaucratic deadline we will hold"](https://discuss.python.org/t/an-announcement-from-the-steering-council-regarding-the-jit-project/107638).

[LWN.net](https://lwn.net/Articles/1102102/) reports that PEP 836 was published on July 3 and that a September 21 Council statement said the PEP "mostly answers the questions we asked" while asking for more discussion before the Council would be asked to pronounce on it. On October 19, Savannah Ostrowski announced the withdrawal: "The Steering Council rightly sets a high bar for a proposal of this scope, and we don't feel we have the personal bandwidth to carry the current version forward." LWN reports that Brett Cannon said the work would stop in the main repository and that it would be up to the community whether it continues elsewhere. LWN adds that the JIT "will likely be removed from CPython main fairly soon," and that it is unclear whether the original developers intend to keep working on it.

[InfoWorld](https://www.infoworld.com/article/4241003/python-jettisons-the-native-jit-at-least-for-now.html), which says its account follows reporting at LWN.net, begins differently: the JIT "will be removed after its maintainers missed deadlines for its formalization set by the Python Steering Council." The Herald's own date arithmetic: a six-month window counted from June 5 would run to early December, later than the October 19 withdrawal. LWN's article, as reviewed, does not describe a missed deadline.

**Kubernetes: version numbers.** The project's 1.37 release post says it has retired the kube-dns subproject and that [no new packages will be built for kube-dns after v1.40](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/26/kubernetes-v1-37-release/), and tells operators to plan migration to CoreDNS. For kube-proxy it says ipvs mode is expected to be disabled by default by v1.40 and that support "would be removed entirely" by v1.43, and that clusters in that mode now log a deprecation warning on startup. For cgroup v1 it says the `failCgroupV1` setting has defaulted to true since v1.35, so the kubelet fails to initialize on cgroup v1 nodes unless overridden, that the override is "a short-term fix," and that removal is planned for a future release, with no version given in that passage. The post's reasons are technical: kube-dns "has not kept pace," and "the kernel ipvs API alone cannot fully implement Kubernetes Services." Its IPVS passage names no replacement mode.

[The Register](https://www.theregister.com/devops/2026/08/26/kubernetes-cleans-house-bins-legacy-kube-dns-ipvs-and-cgroup-v1/5292717) reports the same items. Its wording on kube-dns differs from the project's: it says those running kube-dns "must update their clusters before Kubernetes 1.40, or they will stop working." It also writes that "nftables has now been decreed as the way forward" for kube-proxy. Neither source gives calendar dates for v1.40 or v1.43.

## Implications

The points below are what the cited sources support or what follows from comparing them. They are not predictions.

**Notice is measured in different units.** Node.js states months and years in a table. Microsoft states a date and ties it to a 12-month policy minimum. The Python Steering Council stated six months and a post in the same thread described it as an anchor rather than a strict deadline. The Kubernetes project states release numbers. The Herald's reading of these sources is that only the Node.js and Microsoft cases carry calendar dates for the end, so a reader comparing the four has to convert the Kubernetes targets, and the sources reviewed do not supply the conversion.

**Maintenance capacity appears in the sources for three of the four.** The Herald's tally from the sources above: the Node.js post cites the difficulty of sustaining four or five release lines; The Register attributes the cost of maintenance and compliance to Roth in the ASP.NET Core 2.3 case; and in the CPython case the Steering Council called maintenance "a real concern" in its request while Ostrowski cited "personal bandwidth" in withdrawing the PEP. The Kubernetes post, by contrast, gives technical reasons for the three components. The sources do not show whether capacity was the deciding factor in any case.

**Named alternatives differ in kind.** Node.js says users who already take only LTS releases will see little change beyond version numbering. Microsoft names .NET 10 (LTS) and GitHub Copilot modernization for the migration. Kubernetes names CoreDNS for kube-dns and cgroup v2 for cgroup v1, but its IPVS passage names no replacement. For the JIT, the Council's announcement says development would continue outside the main repository, and [InfoWorld](https://www.infoworld.com/article/4241003/python-jettisons-the-native-jit-at-least-for-now.html) says other developers may continue the work in an alternative build and lists PyPy, CinderX and CPython's adaptive interpreter as other performance efforts.

**Reported friction centres on two of the four.** [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/06/nodejs-release-changes/) reports the enterprise-versus-frequent-upgrader tension in the Node.js discussion, and [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/software/2026/04/08/microsoft-calls-time-on-aspnet-core-23-on-net-framework/5223824) quotes a user objecting in the ASP.NET Core 2.3 case. The Kubernetes post and The Register's Kubernetes article, as reviewed, report no user reaction to the kube-dns, IPVS or cgroup v1 timelines.

**Sources can differ on the same event.** Three differences appear in the reporting reviewed: the ASP.NET Core 2.3 end date (April 7, 2027 in The Register, April 13, 2027 in Microsoft's updated post), the framing of the JIT's removal (InfoWorld's lead says maintainers missed deadlines; the Council thread calls the six-month window flexible, and LWN dates the withdrawal to October 19), and the consequence of staying on kube-dns (no new packages after v1.40 in the project's post, "they will stop working" in The Register). The sources do not say whether the kube-dns difference reflects a technical distinction or a paraphrase.

**What the sources do not establish.** They do not give calendar dates for Kubernetes v1.40 or v1.43, a version for cgroup v1 removal, or counts of users still on ASP.NET Core 2.3, kube-dns or IPVS mode. As of their publication dates they do not say whether the JIT has been removed from the main branch, whether anyone will continue it elsewhere, or how the Node.js Alpha channel has been received by library authors.
